statement: Multi-objective search algorithm comparison (NSGA-II vs random) requires both a non-trivial Pareto frontier AND a sparse Pareto-optimal configuration set. When many configurations per tier achieve equivalent frontier-level objectives, all search algorithms converge identically fast because the frontier is trivially accessible to random sampling. In BLIS's 4-obj KV-constrained space, Pareto density drops to ~12-23% (vs 65% for 3-obj), which is hard enough to give NSGA-II a final quality advantage (+4.4% HV) but insufficient for a clear convergence speed advantage at 200 evals.
regime: BLIS multi-objective search with budget=200 evaluations on GPU configuration space
mechanism: At 65% Pareto density (3-obj, 1M blocks), any 40 random configs reliably cover all Pareto-level objectives. At 12-23% density (4-obj, kv_blocks searchable), random needs more evals to cover the space but 200 evals is sufficient. NSGA-II's crossover advantage materializes as final quality improvement (finding the narrow tp+blocks sweet spots more reliably) but not convergence speed because random covers enough of the space at 200 evals.
applicability_bounds: Applies when: budget ≥ 150 evals, parameter space has 5+ non-informative parameters (routing, block_size, gpu_mem), and the search space has a small number of distinct GPU tiers (<10) that each dominate a region of the Pareto front. May not apply with larger budgets (500+) where cumulative advantage compounds, or with more tightly interacting parameters.

statement: Before running a search algorithm comparison on BLIS, validate BOTH objective diversity (5x variation across configs) AND Pareto set density. For the 3-objective space (no kv_blocks): Pareto density is ~65%, making all algorithms equivalent. For the 4-objective KV-constrained space: density is ~12-23%, enabling NSGA-II's final quality advantage (+4-5%) but insufficient for convergence speed advantage at 200 evals. A density threshold of <<5% per GPU tier likely needed for clear convergence speed gap.
regime: BLIS multi-objective search, rate=50 req/s, qwen/qwen3-14b on H100, budget=200 evals
mechanism: Pareto density is driven by how many parameters meaningfully differentiate configs within the same GPU tier. In 3-obj (no kv_blocks): batch≥256 makes ~60% of configs equivalent. In 4-obj (kv_blocks varies 2k-10k): the blocks×TP interaction creates genuinely different Pareto points, reducing density to 12-23%.
applicability_bounds: Applies when evaluating whether to run a search experiment. Density should be estimated from a small pilot sample (40-50 evals) before committing to full experiment.

statement: In the BLIS configuration space, TP, num_instances, AND total_kv_blocks are dominant parameters when kv_blocks is constrained (below natural threshold). All other parameters (scheduler, routing_policy, block_size, gpu_memory_utilization) remain secondary differentiators affecting metrics only in specific regimes. Non-differentiating parameters inflate search space and dilute NSGA-II's crossover signal, reducing its convergence speed advantage relative to random.
regime: BLIS, rate=50 req/s, qwen/qwen3-14b, H100, kv_blocks in [2000, 10000]
mechanism: TP controls per-step compute speed; num_instances controls total KV capacity (blocks × instances); kv_blocks controls per-instance capacity and determines whether a given (tp, inst) combination is KV-stressed. These three jointly determine the rps/ttft/gpu_count/blocks Pareto tradeoff. Scheduler differentiates only under KV stress (<5% effect overall); routing policy differentiates by <3%; block_size and gpu_mem have negligible effects in this regime.
applicability_bounds: Applies when rate=50 req/s with qwen/qwen3-14b at default workload (prefix_tokens=512). At different rates or model sizes, the binding constraint may shift (e.g., compute-bound at lower rates). Scheduler may differentiate more strongly with heterogeneous request sizes.

statement: NSGA-II's convergence advantage over random search on BLIS manifests as final solution QUALITY improvement (+4-5% hypervolume, 2x Pareto solutions at 200 evals), not as convergence SPEED advantage. Using a shared reference (NSGA-II's final HV), NSGA-II reaches 95% one generation (40 evals) earlier than random. Using own-final reference, both algorithms converge in the same number of evaluations (~eval=120 for 95%). The quality advantage increases as the search budget grows beyond the initial plateau.
regime: BLIS 4-objective KV-constrained space, NSGA-II pop=40 gen=4 vs random at 200 evals total
mechanism: NSGA-II's selection pressure concentrates evaluations near the true Pareto frontier after generation 1-2, finding narrow sweet spots (e.g., tp=4,blocks=8000-10000 for high-rps configs; tp=2,inst=2,blocks=4000-5000 for low-ttft configs). Random spreads evaluations uniformly, covering most sweet spots but missing the finest granularity. By eval=200, NSGA-II has explored the frontier more thoroughly (46 vs 23 Pareto solutions), explaining the quality gap without a speed gap.
applicability_bounds: At budget=200 evals. Quality advantage may grow with budget (500+ evals) as NSGA-II continues refining while random plateaus. May not hold on lower-dimensional spaces where 200 random evals cover the space fully.

statement: Adding total_kv_blocks as a searchable parameter in BLIS's 4-objective formulation reduces Pareto density from ~65% (3-obj, 1M blocks) to ~12-23% (4-obj, blocks in [2k-10k]) and introduces genuine Pareto tradeoffs within the same GPU tier (e.g., tp=4,inst=1 dominates tp=2,inst=2 on rps but is dominated on ttft when blocks are constrained). This creates a qualitatively harder search problem, but at budget=200 evals and with 5 non-differentiating parameters, the hardness is insufficient for a clear NSGA-II convergence speed advantage. Reducing the non-differentiating parameters (routing, block_size, gpu_mem) or increasing the budget to 500+ evals would likely expose a clear gap.
regime: BLIS 4-objective search with kv_blocks in [2000, 10000], rate=50, qwen/qwen3-14b, H100
mechanism: The kv_blocks dimension creates a non-linear interaction: optimal blocks value depends on the tp/instances configuration (per-instance storage, so tp=4,inst=1 needs 2x blocks vs tp=2,inst=2 for the same total capacity). This is a conditional interaction that NSGA-II's crossover can exploit once it identifies good (tp, blocks) pairings. However, 5 non-differentiating parameters add noise that partially masks this signal.
applicability_bounds: Holds for the specific parameter space tested. If non-differentiating parameters (routing, block_size, gpu_mem) are removed (reduced to tp, num_instances, scheduler, max_batch, kv_blocks = ~180 effective configs), the problem is harder for random and NSGA-II's advantage should be clearer. The tradeoff structure also depends on the rate and workload: at different rates, the KV cliff positions shift.
